title: Who Is Anima Anandkumar? The Mysore-Born Scientist Who Turned Down a Bezos-Backed Fortune — and Is Building AI That Understands Physics, Not Words
excerpt: <pWhile the world obsesses over chatbots that write essays and generate code, Anima Anandkumar is quietly building something far more ambitious: artificial intelligence that can understand the physical universe itself…
body:
While the world obsesses over chatbots that write essays and generate code, Anima Anandkumar is quietly building something far more ambitious: artificial intelligence that can understand the physical universe itself.

https://x.com/nordicinst/status/2093859162841039230

Last week, the Mysore-born Caltech professor was named to TIME's 2026 list of the 100 most influential people in AI. Days earlier, she and her husband Benedikt Jenik publicly launched Accelerated Understanding, a Pasadena-based startup whose AI can process 5 trillion data points in a single prompt — roughly 5 million times what ChatGPT or Claude can handle in one sitting.

The catch? Their system doesn't understand language. It understands physics.

"The language-centric view of intelligence is humans at the center," Anandkumar told Reuters. "Putting physics at the center is a nature-centric view."

From Mysore to the Frontier of AI

Animashree "Anima" Anandkumar was born in Mysore, Karnataka, into a family steeped in scholarship. Both her parents are engineers. Her grandfather was a mathematician. And her great-great-grandfather was R. Shamasastry, the Sanskrit scholar who rediscovered the Arthashastra — Kautilya's ancient treatise on statecraft — in 1905, an achievement that reshaped the study of Indian political philosophy.

""The language-centric view of intelligence is humans at the center," Anandkumar told Reuters."

Growing up, Anandkumar trained in Bharatanatyam for years, but it was engineering that called. She earned her B.Tech in Electrical Engineering from IIT Madras in 2004, then headed to Cornell University for her PhD, which she completed in 2009. A postdoctoral stint at MIT followed, where she worked in the Stochastic Systems Group — and a trajectory through the most elite institutions in American AI research was set.

Amazon, Nvidia, and the Road to Neural Operators

After rising from assistant professor at UC Irvine to principal scientist at Amazon Web Services, Anandkumar joined Nvidia in 2018 as senior director of AI research. The same year, Caltech appointed her the Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences — making her, at the time, the youngest named professor at the institution.

At Nvidia, she led a team that pioneered neural operators, a deep learning framework designed not for language but for modeling physical phenomena — fluid dynamics, wave propagation, material behavior. The breakthrough was dramatic: her AI-based weather models ran tens of thousands of times faster than the numerical forecasting systems used by meteorological agencies around the world, with comparable accuracy.

The work caught the eye of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who personally presented Anandkumar's neural operator research at Nvidia's GTC Conference in 2021. When she mentioned how AI could eat physics theorists' lunch, Huang replied: "I want it to eat all their lunches."

Turning Down Bezos

In late 2024, Anandkumar and Jenik were approached about leading Project Prometheus, a venture backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. According to an offer letter reviewed by Reuters, the deal would have made Anandkumar the public face and board member of a company with more than $2 billion in committed funding. The package included a 35% stake and a $1 million annual salary that would double to $2 million after three months.

They walked away.

While Bezos and co-founder Vik Bajaj went on to raise a $12 billion Series B for Prometheus in June 2026, Anandkumar and Jenik chose to build Accelerated Understanding on their own terms. The company launched publicly on August 25, with enterprise clients as its initial focus — using one generalized AI system for chip design, robotics, extreme weather prediction, and geological data analysis.

"Instead of brittle and bespoke math models for each, one AI can handle any physics query for the business world," Anandkumar said.

Awards, Advocacy, and Changing a Conference's Name

Anandkumar's accolades read like a highlight reel of the field's most prestigious honors: Fellow of the IEEE, ACM, and AAAI; Guggenheim Fellow; Blavatnik Award for Young Scientists; TIME100 Impact Award; the ACM Gordon Bell Special Prize; and now, TIME100 AI Innovator for 2026. She has presented her work on AI for science to the White House's Presidential Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) and at TED 2024.

But her influence extends beyond research. Anandkumar has been a vocal advocate for gender equity in STEM. She launched a petition calling on IIT Madras to end gender segregation in its admissions process and strengthen campus protections against sexual harassment. She was one of the campaigners who successfully pushed to rename the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems from its original abbreviation, "NIPS," to NeurIPS.

Why She Matters to the Diaspora

In a year when ten Indians and Indian-origin leaders made TIME's AI 100 list, Anandkumar stands out for charting her own path. She didn't take the biggest check on the table. She didn't follow the playbook of building another language model. Instead, the Mysore girl who grew up with a mathematician grandfather and a freedom-era Sanskrit scholar in her family tree is building AI that speaks the language of nature itself — from weather systems to nuclear fusion to the materials inside the chips that power our phones.

At a moment when the AI industry is saturated with hype, Anandkumar's bet is a contrarian one: that the most important intelligence isn't the kind that writes your emails. It's the kind that understands the universe.
